vopros: What do foreign nationals need to buy a home in Los Angeles?

vyzhimka.tekst:
Yes. Foreign nationals can generally buy residential real estate in Los Angeles; U.S. citizenship or permanent residency is not generally a prerequisite. The main differences are financing, documentation, taxes, and how you structure ownership.

For a typical purchase, you should expect to need:

- Identification: A valid foreign passport and often a second form of ID. You don't need a green card simply to own the property.
- Purchase funds: For a cash purchase, you'll need documentation showing where the money came from and the ability to wire it through the banking/escrow system. Banks, escrow companies, and title companies may require extensive identity and source-of-funds documentation.
- Financing, if applicable: Foreign-national mortgages exist, but lenders set their own requirements. Compared with conventional U.S. borrowers, foreign buyers frequently face larger down payments and more documentation of overseas income, assets, bank accounts, and credit history. The exact requirements depend heavily on the lender and your immigration/residency status.
- U.S. tax planning: Owning U.S. real estate can create U.S. federal and California tax consequences, particularly if you rent the home or eventually sell it. California-source rental income can be subject to California taxation and nonresident withholding rules. ([ftb.ca.gov](https://www.ftb.ca.gov/pay/withholding/withholding-on-nonresidents.html?utm_source=openai))
- Escrow/title paperwork: California purchases ordinarily go through an escrow/title process. The buyer will need to provide whatever identification and compliance documentation those institutions require.
- Ownership structure: You can potentially purchase individually or through certain entities/trust arrangements, but a foreign buyer should get tax advice before choosing an LLC, corporation, trust, or joint ownership simply for liability or estate-planning reasons. Cross-border tax consequences can make seemingly simple structures surprisingly expensive.

One especially important issue is what happens later when a foreign owner sells. Under FIRPTA, when a "foreign person" sells U.S. real property, the buyer generally has to withhold 15% of the amount realized, subject to exceptions and procedures for reducing withholding. This is withholding toward tax—not necessarily the seller's actual tax liability. ([irs.gov](https://www.irs.gov/individuals/international-taxpayers/firpta-withholding?utm_source=openai)) California also has its own real-estate withholding regime; foreign sellers generally follow the California rules applicable to sellers. ([ftb.ca.gov](https://www.ftb.ca.gov/pay/withholding/real-estate-withholding.html?utm_source=openai))

An ITIN is not necessarily something you must already possess simply to purchase a house for cash. Tax identification becomes relevant depending on your tax filing, rental, financing, and eventual-sale circumstances; the IRS specifically notes that merely planning to own/sell real estate isn't automatically a basis to obtain an ITIN before there's a qualifying tax reason. ([irs.gov](https://www.irs.gov/individuals/international-taxpayers/firpta-withholding?utm_source=openai))

If you're considering, for example, a $1–3 million Los Angeles home as a non-U.S. citizen living abroad, I can also walk you through a realistic example covering the down payment, foreign-national mortgage, closing costs, annual property taxes, and U.S./California tax considerations.
